AI coding tools changed how my team works, but not in the way I expected. The engineers who benefit most are the ones who already write clear tickets and small pull requests. AI amplifies your habits. If your habits are messy, you just get mess faster. ## Related - [[what-ai-coding-tools-changed-in-my-team]] - [[my-first-90-days-as-an-engineering-lead]] - [[how-to-measure-a-platform-team]]

chunks.title: Audit your meetings every quarter
chunks.text: Audit your meetings every quarter. # Audit your meetings every quarter Meetings multiply quietly. Each one made sense when it was created, and nobody ever deletes them. Every quarter I audit my team's recurring meetings with three questions. What decision or outcome did this meeting produce in the last month? Could it be a written update instead? Who attends but never speaks? Last quarter the audit removed four recurring meetings and shortened two more. That gave every engineer back about three hours a week, which is nearly two working weeks a quarter per person. The meetings that survive are the ones where people need to think together: design reviews, retrospectives and one-to-ones. Status updates moved to writing, where they're faster to read and easier to search.

chunks.title: Blameless postmortems that actually change things
chunks.text: Blameless postmortems that actually change things. # Blameless postmortems that actually change things Blameless postmortems that actually change things Created on 2026-02-10 Every team I've joined says it runs blameless postmortems. Few of them change anything afterwards. The document gets written, the meeting happens, and three months later the same outage comes back wearing a different hat. Blameless does not mean actionless. A good postmortem answers three questions: what happened, why it made sense to the people involved at the time, and what we will change so that the next person in the same situation succeeds. The second question is the one teams skip. If you don't understand why a reasonable engineer ran that command, you will write an action item like 'be more careful', which is not an action item. It is a wish. My rule: every postmortem must produce at most three actions, each with an owner and a date, and at least one must change a system rather than a person. chunks.title: Code review is not a gate, it's a conversation.
chunks.text: Code review is not a gate, it's a conversation.. # Code review is not a gate, it's a conversation. Code review is not a gate, it's a conversation. When my team started treating reviews as 'approve or block', cycle time went up and trust went down. We changed one thing: every review must start with what the author did well and one question before any request. Within a month, median review time dropped from 26 hours to 9, and people started asking for reviews earlier instead of hiding big pull requests.

chunks.title: Hiring for curiosity
chunks.text: Hiring for curiosity. # Hiring for curiosity Skills go out of date. Curiosity doesn't. When I hire engineers, I look hard for evidence that someone keeps learning without being told to. In interviews I ask about the last thing they learned that wasn't required for their job, and how they learned it. I ask them to explain a system they've worked on to someone non-technical. And I ask what they would do in their first week if they joined a team with a codebase they'd never seen. Strong answers are specific. They name a book, a side project, a bug they chased for days because they wanted to understand it. Weak answers are general: I like learning new things. Curious engineers ask better questions in design reviews, debug faster and adapt to new tools quickly. In a year where AI tools change every month, curiosity has become the skill that predicts all the others. ## Related - [[ive-interviewed-over-200-engineers]] - [[how-i-grow-senior-engineers]] - [[what-i-tell-junior-engineers]]

chunks.title: Hot take: most 'platform teams' fail because they build what's...
chunks.text: Hot take: most 'platform teams' fail because they build what's.... # Hot take: most 'platform teams' fail because they build what's... Hot take: most 'platform teams' fail because they build what's interesting, not what's adopted. My test for any internal tool: would a team choose it if it were optional? If the answer is no, you're not building a platform, you're building a mandate. ## Related - [[how-to-measure-a-platform-team]] - [[why-engineering-teams-should-write-more]]

chunks.title: How I grow senior engineers
chunks.text: How I grow senior engineers. # How I grow senior engineers How I grow senior engineers Created on 2026-05-28 Promotion to senior is not a reward for writing more code. It's recognition that someone makes the people around them better. When I coach engineers towards senior, I look for three shifts. First, from solving the problem in front of them to asking whether it's the right problem. Second, from owning their code to owning an outcome, including the boring parts like monitoring and documentation. Third, from being helped to helping: reviewing well, unblocking others, and explaining decisions in writing. The fastest way I know to build these habits is to give someone a small, real project with a fuzzy edge: a migration nobody owns, a flaky service, a process that annoys everyone. Then I stay close but don't steer. The fuzzy edge is where judgement grows. I also ask every senior on my team to write one short internal post a month about something they learned. Writing forces clarity, and it scales their influence beyond the meetings they attend. ## Related - [[ive-interviewed-over-200-engineers]] - [[writing-a-design-doc-is-not-about-the-doc]]

chunks.title: How to measure a platform team
chunks.text: How to measure a platform team. # How to measure a platform team Platform teams struggle to show their value because their best work is invisible: things simply stop breaking and start being easy. I measure platform success with adoption and time, not output. How many teams use the platform when they could choose not to? How long does it take a new service to go from idea to production? How long does a new engineer take to ship their first change? When we started tracking time to first production deploy for new services, it was 11 days. After a year of platform work it was under 2. That single number told leadership more than any list of features we'd built. Pick two or three numbers that your users would care about, measure them honestly, and share them every month. If they don't move, change what you're building. ## Related - [[hot-take-most-platform-teams-fail-because-they-build-whats]] - [[ai-coding-tools-changed-how-my-team-works-but-not-in-the-way-i]] - [[what-ai-coding-tools-changed-in-my-team]]

chunks.text: I've interviewed over 200 engineers.. # I've interviewed over 200 engineers. I've interviewed over 200 engineers. The signal I trust most isn't the algorithm question. It's how someone talks about a bug they caused. People who can describe their own mistake calmly, with what they learned and what they changed, tend to be the ones who make teams safer. ## Related - [[how-i-grow-senior-engineers]] - [[hiring-for-curiosity]] - [[what-i-tell-junior-engineers]]

chunks.title: My first 90 days as an engineering lead
chunks.text: My first 90 days as an engineering lead. # My first 90 days as an engineering lead When I stepped up to lead a team for the first time, I made the classic mistake: I kept coding as much as before and treated leadership as extra work on top. What finally worked was a 90-day plan in three parts. In the first 30 days I listened: one-to-ones with every engineer, every stakeholder, and the support team who hear customer pain first. In the next 30 days I fixed one visible thing the team had complained about for months, which for us was a flaky test suite. That bought trust. In the last 30 days I set out a simple direction for the next two quarters and wrote it down. The lesson I'd pass on: your job is no longer to be the best engineer in the room. It's to make the room work. Coding becomes something you do when it unblocks others, not when it's the most fun task available. ## Related - [[ai-coding-tools-changed-how-my-team-works-but-not-in-the-way-i]] - [[what-ai-coding-tools-changed-in-my-team]] - [[how-to-measure-a-platform-team]]

chunks.title: New managers often ask me how to run 1:1s.
chunks.text: New managers often ask me how to run 1:1s.. # New managers often ask me how to run 1:1s. New managers often ask me how to run 1:1s. Mine have three questions that never change: What's on your mind? What's getting in your way? What do you want to be doing more of in six months? The third one is where careers actually get shaped.

chunks.title: On-call without burnout
chunks.text: On-call without burnout. # On-call without burnout On-call is where engineering culture shows its real face. A team can talk about wellbeing all day, but if the same three people carry the pager every holiday, everyone knows what the team actually values. My rules for a healthy rotation are simple. Every engineer who ships to production joins the rotation, including leads. Shifts are one week, with a proper handover note. Anyone paged at night starts late the next day, no questions asked. And every page gets a short review on Monday: was it real, was it actionable, and could a machine have handled it? The Monday review is what changes things. Alerts that aren't actionable get deleted or downgraded. Repeat pages become sprint work. Within two quarters, our out-of-hours pages fell from around 30 a month to fewer than 8. On-call should be boring. If it's exciting, your system is telling you something. ## Related - [[the-best-on-call-rotation-i-ever-ran-had-a-rule-if-you-get-paged]] - [[saying-no-to-stakeholders-without-losing-them]]

chunks.title: Psychological safety starts in the incident channel
chunks.text: Psychological safety starts in the incident channel. # Psychological safety starts in the incident channel You can tell how safe a team feels by reading its incident channel during an outage. In unsafe teams, people hesitate. They wait to be sure before saying anything, because being wrong in public feels costly. Meanwhile the outage continues. In safe teams, people say what they see as soon as they see it, including 'I just deployed something, could it be me?' That one sentence can cut an outage from an hour to five minutes. Leaders create this safety by how they react in the first moments. Thank people for raising things early. Never ask 'who did this?' during an incident. Ask 'what do we know?' and 'what are we trying next?'. Save the learning for the postmortem, and keep that blameless too. Safety isn't a poster on the wall. It's what happens to the first person who admits a mistake.

chunks.title: Saying no to stakeholders without losing them
chunks.text: Saying no to stakeholders without losing them. # Saying no to stakeholders without losing them Saying no to stakeholders without losing them Created on 2026-10-01 Engineering leads spend a surprising amount of time saying no. Done badly, it burns trust. Done well, it builds it. I never say a plain no. I say what we would have to stop doing to say yes, and I let the stakeholder weigh it with me. Most of the time they choose the existing priority themselves, and they leave the meeting feeling heard rather than blocked. The second habit is to write it down. A two-line message after the meeting, 'we agreed to keep X ahead of Y until the end of the quarter', prevents the same conversation from happening every week. Finally, give a real date for when you'll revisit. 'Not now' with a date is a plan. 'Not now' without one is a brush-off, and people can tell the difference. ## Related - [[on-call-without-burnout]]

chunks.title: The best on-call rotation I ever ran had a rule: if you get paged...
chunks.text: The best on-call rotation I ever ran had a rule: if you get paged.... # The best on-call rotation I ever ran had a rule: if you get paged... The best on-call rotation I ever ran had a rule: if you get paged twice for the same thing, fixing it becomes the top priority for the next sprint. Not a ticket in the backlog. The top priority. Pages are a tax your past self charges your future self, and someone has to stop paying it. ## Related - [[on-call-without-burnout]]

chunks.title: The case for small pull requests
chunks.text: The case for small pull requests. # The case for small pull requests The case for small pull requests Created on 2026-08-19 If I could change one habit across every engineering team I've worked with, it would be the size of pull requests. Large pull requests are slow to review, so they wait. While they wait, they drift from the main branch, so they conflict. When they're finally reviewed, reviewers skim, because nobody can hold 1,500 lines in their head. Bugs get through, and the author feels the review was a formality. Small pull requests, under about 200 lines, flip all of this. They get reviewed within hours, reviewers actually read them, and if something breaks it's easy to find and revert. The objection I hear is that some changes are big. They are. But a big change can almost always be shipped as a series of small, safe steps behind a feature flag. Learning to slice work this way is one of the most valuable skills an engineer can build, and it's a skill AI coding tools make even more important.

chunks.title: Treat technical debt like a budget
chunks.text: Treat technical debt like a budget. # Treat technical debt like a budget Arguing about technical debt in every planning meeting wastes everyone's energy. On my teams we agreed a budget instead: about 20 percent of each sprint goes to reducing debt, and the engineers decide how to spend it. The budget works because it removes the fight. Product managers know the time is reserved, so they plan around it. Engineers know they don't need permission for each fix, so they pick the debt that hurts most today. We keep a short list of debt items ranked by pain: how often it slows us down, how often it causes incidents, and how scary it is to change. Every quarter we look back at what the budget bought us. Usually it's faster builds, fewer pages and happier new joiners, which is an easy story to tell leadership. Debt isn't bad. Unmanaged debt is.

chunks.title: We cut our deploy time from 40 minutes to 6.
chunks.text: We cut our deploy time from 40 minutes to 6.. # We cut our deploy time from 40 minutes to 6. We cut our deploy time from 40 minutes to 6. The biggest win wasn't caching or parallel tests. It was deleting 300 tests that had not failed in two years and tested nothing anyone cared about. Every test is a promise you keep paying for. Audit your promises.

chunks.title: What AI coding tools changed in my team
chunks.text: What AI coding tools changed in my team. # What AI coding tools changed in my team We've used AI coding assistants on my team for over a year now. The honest summary: they made good habits more valuable and bad habits more expensive. Engineers who break work into small, clear tasks get great results. The assistant writes the boilerplate, suggests tests and catches silly mistakes. Engineers who start with a vague goal get large, plausible-looking changes that are hard to review and sometimes subtly wrong. So we changed how we work, not just which tools we use. Every task starts with a short written intent: what should change and how we'll know it worked. Pull requests stay small. Reviewers ask the author to explain any AI-written code they don't fully understand. And we keep a shared file of instructions for the assistant, describing our conventions, so it writes code that fits. AI didn't replace engineering judgement. It raised the price of not having it. ## Related - [[ai-coding-tools-changed-how-my-team-works-but-not-in-the-way-i]] - [[my-first-90-days-as-an-engineering-lead]] - [[how-to-measure-a-platform-team]]

chunks.title: What I tell junior engineers
chunks.text: What I tell junior engineers. # What I tell junior engineers Every few months a junior engineer asks me what they should focus on. My answer has barely changed in ten years. Read more code than you write. Pick a well-run open-source project and read how they structure things, name things and review things. Ask questions early. A question after 30 minutes of being stuck is a sign of good judgement, not weakness. A question after three days is a missed deadline. Learn to debug methodically: reproduce, isolate, form one hypothesis at a time, and write down what you've ruled out. And write down what you learn. A simple notes file of problems and solutions becomes, after a year, the most useful document you own. It's also, I've discovered, the start of a personal knowledge base that AI tools can work with. ## Related - [[ive-interviewed-over-200-engineers]] - [[how-i-grow-senior-engineers]] - [[hiring-for-curiosity]]

chunks.title: Why engineering teams should write more
chunks.text: Why engineering teams should write more. # Why engineering teams should write more The highest-leverage habit in a distributed team is writing. Not more documentation for its own sake, but writing as a way to think and decide. When a decision lives only in a meeting, it lives only in the memories of the people who attended, and memories drift. When it lives in a short written note, new joiners can find it, people in other time zones can comment on it, and future you can understand why past you chose it. I ask for three kinds of writing on my teams: design docs for anything that takes more than two weeks, decision records for choices we might regret, and short weekly updates that say what shipped, what's blocked and what's next. The pushback is always time. But a one-page doc that takes an hour to write saves several hours of meetings and weeks of rework. Writing is not overhead. It's how a team remembers. ## Related - [[hot-take-most-platform-teams-fail-because-they-build-whats]] - [[writing-a-design-doc-is-not-about-the-doc]] - [[how-i-grow-senior-engineers]]

chunks.title: Writing a design doc is not about the doc.
chunks.text: Writing a design doc is not about the doc.. # Writing a design doc is not about the doc. Writing a design doc is not about the doc. It's about finding the disagreement early, when it's cheap. My template has one section people skip and shouldn't: 'What would make this the wrong decision?' Fill that in honestly and half your review meeting is already done. ## Related - [[how-i-grow-senior-engineers]] - [[why-engineering-teams-should-write-more]]
